name: Udihe
catalog_quote: The stress is quantity-sensitive and falls on the most right bimoraic vowel or, in the absence of bimoraic vowels, on the most right vowel in the word. In affixes, word-final high vowels are extrametrical with respect to stress.

audit.recode_to: weight (default: rightmost/final vowel; heavy = bimoraic vowel, i.e. long or laryngealized; rightmost heavy wins, unbounded; word-final short high vowels of inflectional affixes extrametrical -> penult in such forms; optional srule/caution: Soviet tradition (Sunik 1968:213, Kormushin 1998) describes weak expiratory/dynamic initial prominence plus final pitch rise, Kormushin calling the initial one 'the stress proper'). If the catalog will not carry a weight rule without §3.6.3 in hand, interim kind should be weight-hedged or conflict, not fixed-strict.
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the N&T 2001:33 sentence is verbatim in the held preview PDF at the stated page (PDF p. 67, running head check OK); Sunik 1968:213 and Tolskaya 2011:26 quotes also confirmed in held files. (2) But the classification does not rest on that quote: kind 'fixed-strict', rule_class 'dual' (final primary + initial secondary, quantity-insensitive) is the StressTyp2/Gordon 2002 label, built on Kormushin 1998 as read by Gordon. The held primaries disagree with it in two directions: Kormushin 1998 and Sunik 1968 make the initial syllable the dynamic stress and the final a pitch rise (Gordon inverted primary/secondary), while the modern fieldwork grammar N&T 2001 (and co-author Tolskaya 2011 with worked examples á:n.ta, ni.m'áŋ.ku.we.ni) states an unbounded quantity-sensitive rule, rightmost bimoraic vowel else final, with affix-final high-vowel extrametricality; N&T's own text uses stres

sources.quote: 'The primary stress in Udihe falls on the final vowel, unless the word contains one or more bimoraic syllables (with long and laryngealized vowels). In this case, the stress falls on the rightmost bimoraic syllable: ab.u.gá "father"; á:n.ta "woman"; ni.m'áŋ.ku.we.ni "his tale (ACC)"; a:k.ta.ma.sié.me.ni "chasing (ACC)." The stressed vowel is usually marked by greater intensity and sometimes by pitch raising and lengthening. ... Secondary stress is less intense and in polysyllabic words can fall on the last syllable. Word-final syllables with high vowels (/i/ and /u/) in inflectional affixes an
